transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-09-09
- Start: 14:00 UTC
- Duration: 47m
- Recording: yes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair, Carlos Mendes, Leah Brooks (Solstice)

Summary:
Weekly check-in for the TurboQueue POC. Reviewed last week's runbook changes (continuous batching ON, queue depth targets), looked at micro-bench numbers, talked about p99 spikes and backpressure behavior under burst, decided on targeted bench and next tuning steps.

Topics:
- Continuous batching behavior and batch size distribution
- Concurrency targets and queueing thresholds
- KV cache warmup and cold-start impact
- Burst smoothing and fallback model variants
Action items & Quick notes:
- See action_items field for owners/due dates
Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — we'll run through the last bench, tune suggestions, and agree next steps. hi Priya, Carlos, Leah.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Hey Maya, yeah thanks. We had, um, some odd p99A spikes on Wednesday when we ran the high-tps sim, so keen to understand whether batching is actually helping or it's just adding latency when the queue floods.
[00:31] Daniel Park: Right, so the data we looked at — and I'll pull up the dashboard after this — shows continuous batching reduced avg token cost by about 18% but p99 increased in two windows where concurrency hit the configured limit. That suggests queue head-of-line blocking.
[01:02] Carlos Mendes: We did set concurrency to 32 per VM, and we have a burst cap to 64 but that kicks in with a kind of blurry fallback. Not sure if the fallback model variant is trimming context in a way that causes more tokens.
[01:22] Leah Brooks: Also worth flagging our SLO: p99 must be < 650ms for interactive routes. Some of the p99s were around 900ms during spike.
[01:35] Maya Chen: Ok yeah that's consistent. Quick clarification — during that run was KV cache warmed? I recall the initial burst test had a cold cache which inflated latency.
[01:44] Priya Nair: There was a mix — the first 10 minutes were cold, then warmed. We used representative prompts but maybe not enough prefix reuse.
[01:55] Daniel Park: Notes from infra: cold KV cache raises token generation time by ~40% in our profile for that model family. For continuous batching, we saw average batch size 4.8, median 3, and tail batches of singletons cause inefficiencies. We can bump batching target to prefer slightly larger batches while keeping a short latency cap.
[02:26] Carlos Mendes: How do you recommend controlling the cap? We don't want latency blowouts.
[02:33] Daniel Park: Two levers — target_batch_size and max_hold_ms. For TurboQueue I'd suggest target 8, max_hold 15ms, and concurrency backpressure threshold at 48. That keeps steady-state under 600ms but still allows bursts.
[02:52] Priya Nair: Sounds plausible. Curious about billing impact though — larger batches but longer hold might increase cost per-request?
[02:59] Maya Chen: Usually batching reduces per-token compute cost; hold introduces a tiny latency to the first token but overall cost drops. We'll model per-1M requests in the playbook.
[03:12] [00:03:12] Priya Nair: Ok. Can you explain the fallback model behavior when we exceed dedicated capacity? We saw the model switch and latencies jump.
[03:22] Daniel Park: The routing policy falls back to a lighter quantized variant that has faster token throughput but lower context window handling; if your prompts rely on long context you may see token churn and re-generation. We can configure an automatic truncation policy or pin critical routes to dedicated capacity so they don't fall through.
[03:48] Carlos Mendes: Pinning is attractive but we need to understand cost delta. For pilot we'd probably pin 20% of traffic.
[03:55] Maya Chen: Noted — I'll include a cost delta for pinned vs fallback in the follow-up.
[04:04] [00:04:04] Leah Brooks: On queueing — we saw a backlog of 700 requests and then a sudden surge cleared it but caused many requests to time out. Are there tuning knobs for smoothing?
[04:17] Daniel Park: Yes — two things: adaptive concurrency (scale up concurrency when backlog rises) and burst smoothing (shed or redirect low-priority traffic). For this POC we can enable adaptive concurrency with conservative growth (20% per 10s) and a low-priority queue for background calls.
[04:41] Priya Nair: Can the low-priority queue be routed to a cheaper quantized model automatically?
[04:47] Daniel Park: Yep, that's the usual pattern: route background/analytics calls to a quantized variant, keep interactive on higher-quality model. We can simulate that in the bench.
[04:56] Maya Chen: Quick check — do you have sample traffic traces we can use for more realistic benching?
[05:01] Carlos Mendes: We're uploading a day's trace now, should be available in the shared bucket by tomorrow morning.
[05:07] Daniel Park: Great — once we have it we'll replay at 1x and 3x to see the queue dynamics.
[05:13] [00:05:13] Priya Nair: For the bench configuration, can you include KV-cache warmup step? We want to see cold->warm transitions realistically.
[05:23] Daniel Park: Yes — bench will include a 10-minute warmup, then three 10-minute windows: steady, spike (3x), and recovery. We'll surface p50/p95/p99 and batch size histogram.
[05:38] Maya Chen: Next — we observed some misattribution in the Fireflies logs where speaker labels were swapped, so the transcript might look odd in places.
[05:47] Priya Nair: Haha that's fine. The important part is the metrics.
[05:51] [00:05:51] Carlos Mendes: One operational question: our infra team prefers VPC endpoints and customer-managed KMS. Is that available for this POC or only in Private deployment?
[06:03] Maya Chen: For the hosted POC we support VPC peering and bring-your-own-KMS for encryption at rest; full on-prem package is a Private deployment but we can give a scoped VPC/KMS setup for the pilot.
[06:17] Leah Brooks: Good. We need audit logs and SSO — most of our compliance checks require SAML and keystroke-level audit.
[06:25] Maya Chen: We can enable SAML SSO and extended audit logs; note extended retention is an add-on per the contract.
[06:32] [00:06:32] Priya Nair: Back to tuning — any suggestion for queue depth thresholds? We saw p99 spike after queue > 500.
[06:41] Daniel Park: Set a soft queue cap at 300, hard cap at 600. Above soft cap, start shedding low-priority traffic and increase concurrency adaptively. The idea is to avoid long head-of-line waits.
[06:55] Carlos Mendes: If we adapt concurrency, do we risk GPU memory pressure?
[07:01] Daniel Park: We tested memory headroom with these settings — at concurrency 48 we still had 15% headroom on our test instance type. But we'll confirm with your exact model and sequence length distribution.
[07:15] [00:07:15] Priya Nair: Sequence lengths are longer for our legal summarization route — median 1.2k tokens. That might change the concurrency targets.
[07:24] Daniel Park: Important note — longer sequence lengths drastically reduce effective concurrency. For those routes we'll recommend lower concurrency and aggressive KV caching. Also consider prefix caching to amortize long context cost.
[07:39] Maya Chen: Can we walk through the micro-bench numbers you saw Thursday, Daniel?
[07:43] Daniel Park: Sure; pulling the slide — average inference latency 210ms, avg tokens per request 86, effective GPU utilization 72%; 95th latency 480ms in steady state; p99 spiked to 920ms during the burst window. Batches had mean size 4.8 as I said.
[08:02] Priya Nair: Were there many singleton batches during the spike?
[08:06] Daniel Park: Yes, around 28% singleton. That's why increasing target batch helps — you want to reduce singleton frequency but not at the expense of adding too much wait time.
[08:19] Maya Chen: For the bench we recommended earlier: target_batch=8, max_hold_ms=15, concurrency_soft=48, concurrency_hard=64, soft_queue=300, hard_queue=600, enable adaptive concurrency with 20% growth per 10s. Do you want us to try a variant with target_batch=12 and max_hold 25ms?
[08:44] Priya Nair: Let's try the primary config first and then the higher-batch variant if we still see singleton tail.
[08:51] Leah Brooks: Also please include a run with KV-cache disabled so we can quantify the warm/cold penalty.
[08:58] Daniel Park: We'll include cold-warm comparison.
[09:02] [00:09:02] Carlos Mendes: On metrics — can Redwood push a detailed trace to our Datadog? Or we pull logs from your console?
[09:10] Maya Chen: We can push ingestion to your Datadog; we can also provide raw logs (JSON) in S3. Which do you prefer?
[09:16] Carlos Mendes: Datadog is ideal for us.
[09:19] Maya Chen: Noted.
[09:22] [00:09:22] Priya Nair: Anything else on tuning?
[09:25] Daniel Park: One more thing — TTL for KV cache entries. With your workload, a TTL of 45 minutes reduces cold misses significantly. We can tune this after seeing the trace.
[09:36] Priya Nair: Great. On timeline, we want to validate steady-state within two sprints. after you run the bench and we review results, we could do a short production pilot with 10% traffic.
[09:49] Maya Chen: That aligns. For procurement, do you have blockers around SOC2 docs or contract terms?
[09:55] Priya Nair: We'll need SOC2 Type II and a standard DPA. Security already started a review.
[09:59] Maya Chen: We'll send SOC2 and DPA.
[10:03] [00:10:03] Daniel Park: Quick note on cost: enabling burst smoothing and pinning will increase committed capacity costs; we'll provide clear per-month delta so you can decide.
[10:12] Priya Nair: ok.
[10:14] Maya Chen: Cool. Let's recap actions and owners.
[10:18] Priya Nair: Quick minor point — during a prior run the model truncated long legal contexts unexpectedly; can Redwood add a guard to error instead of silently trimming?
[10:27] Daniel Park: We can add a validation check to fail the request with a clear error if context length would exceed the pinned model window. That way you know to route or truncate upstream.
[10:36] Carlos Mendes: Useful.
[10:40] [00:10:40] Maya Chen: Recap / next steps: Redwood runs bench with target config and cold->warm; push results + raw logs to S3 and send Datadog integration; Solstice provides traffic trace; Redwood sends tuning playbook and cost delta for pinning/burst; schedule deep-dive if bench shows persistent p99 > 650ms.
[10:58] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone. We'll review bench results when available and pick a date for the production 10% pilot.
[11:06] Maya Chen: Thanks, meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
